beats.intro: Chapter three, lesson one. Water and life. [[glass]]A glass of water looks plain. [[zoom]]But life cannot do without it, and almost everything odd about water starts with one small molecule. [[title]]In this lesson we see why that molecule has two ends, and how it grips its neighbors.
beats.share: Start with the bond. [[h2]]A covalent bond forms when two atoms share a pair of electrons. [[tug]]But sharing is not always fair. Every atom pulls on shared electrons with some strength, and that pull is called electronegativity. [[equal]]Two identical atoms pull equally, so the electrons sit in the middle. [[oh]]Oxygen pulls much harder than hydrogen. So in each oxygen to hydrogen bond, the electrons spend more time near the oxygen.
beats.pull: That uneven sharing leaves a small charge on each atom. [[neg]]Oxygen, which has the electrons more often, is slightly negative. We write that delta minus. [[pos]]Each hydrogen is slightly positive, delta plus. [[partial]]These are partial charges, far smaller than the full charge of an ion. No electron has left, they are only shared unevenly. [[polar]]A bond like this is called a polar covalent bond.
beats.shape: Now the shape. [[bent]]The three atoms do not sit in a line. The two hydrogens sit at an angle of about one hundred five degrees, so the molecule is bent. [[sides]]That puts both positive hydrogens on one side, and the negative oxygen on the other. [[polarmol]]So the whole molecule has a positive end and a negative end. It is a polar molecule. [[line]]If water were straight, the two pulls would point opposite ways and cancel, and there would be no ends at all. [[why]]The bend is why water is polar.
beats.q1: Quick check. Think about the shape.
beats.attract: Now bring two water molecules close. [[rule]]Opposite charges attract. [[near]]The positive hydrogen of one molecule is drawn toward the negative oxygen of its neighbor. [[bond]]That attraction is a hydrogen bond. [[between]]Notice where it sits. It is not inside a molecule. It links one molecule to another. [[solid]]The solid line inside a molecule is a covalent bond, made of shared electrons. The dashed line between molecules is only an attraction.
beats.weak: A hydrogen bond is weak. [[strength]]It is far weaker than the covalent bonds that hold each molecule together. [[jostle]]In liquid water the molecules never stop moving, and the jostling breaks hydrogen bonds again and again. [[swap]]A molecule lets go of one neighbor and bonds to another, in a tiny fraction of a second. [[net]]So the bonds are always changing, yet at any moment most molecules are still joined to several neighbors. [[keep]]The molecules stay whole. Only the hydrogen bonds come and go.
beats.four: How many neighbors can one molecule hold? [[ox]]Oxygen has two pairs of electrons that are not used in bonds. They give it two negative regions, each able to attract a hydrogen from a neighbor. [[hyd]]And the molecule has two positive hydrogens, each able to reach for a neighbor's oxygen. [[count]]Two plus two. One molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds. [[web]]Repeat that across a whole glass, and every molecule is linked into a shifting web.
beats.q2: Quick check. Find the hydrogen bond.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Unequal sharing of electrons makes the bonds in water polar, with oxygen slightly negative and hydrogen slightly positive. [[w2]]Water's bent shape makes the whole molecule polar. [[w3]]Opposite charges on neighboring molecules attract, and that attraction is a hydrogen bond. [[w4]]Each bond is weak and keeps breaking and re-forming, but one molecule can make up to four. [[end]]In the next lessons we see what this web does. It holds water together, steadies its temperature, makes ice float, and lets water dissolve other things. Now try the practice.

beats.finish: Well done. That's the end of lesson one. Next, what all these hydrogen bonds do together.
